source.title: Protecting Privacy in Multimodal Large Language Models with MLLMU-Bench
source.authors: Zheyuan Liu; Guang-Yao Dou; Mengzhao Jia; Zhao-Xuan Tan; Qing-Kai Zeng; Yongle Yuan; Meng Jiang

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some table and figure content is flattened in the supplied text, limiting assignment of individual numeric values.
record.tranche_reason: Tests unlearning efficacy and utility in MLLMs using profile data and classification, generation, and cloze evaluations; these are different settings and measures from the cited LLM unlearning evaluations.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates unlearning methods on target profiles and transformed test examples, and measures retained/general capability. Its paraphrased questions are evaluated together with transformed images, not as a prompting-only recovery attack. The system-prompt baseline is used to prevent disclosure, not to recover knowledge. It reports no recovery experiments using fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information. The cited observation that unlearned models may relearn through in-context learning is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: A new setting (multimodal LLMs, LLaVA-1.5-7B and Idefics2-8B, fictitious-profile forgetting) that reports forget-set accuracy against retain and general utility for GA, Grad. Diff., KL, NPO and prompting. These results bear on whether unlearning reaches near chance while keeping ability (A). No relearning, internal-edit, quantization or isolated prompting attack is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it omits the headline finding. Unimodal (text-only) unlearning forgets better on generation and cloze, while multimodal unlearning forgets better on multimodal classification. Non-modality-aware methods leave incomplete removal across modalities. There is an unlearning–utility trade-off across retain accuracy, neighbouring celebrities, MMMU and LLaVA-Bench.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts established unlearning baselines, including Gradient Ascent, to multimodal privacy-profile data; evaluates classification, generation, and cloze tasks rather than reproducing an original attack-and-recovery procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on modality, task, model, and forget-set proportion; GA’s unlearning effectiveness is accompanied by utility losses.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates in the supplied results. Some results are only available in figures whose values are flattened in the text, preventing reliable assignment of individual numbers. Its paraphrased-question test also changes images, so it cannot isolate prompting-only effects.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were extracted from the flattened Table 2 or Appendix figures because the supplied layout does not reliably map every numerical value to model, split, method, dataset, and metric.

untested.parts: No relearning, activation, quantization, jailbreak or multilingual attacks. Chance level for the multiple-choice items is not stated.
No activation ablation or block-versus-delete analysis.
Paraphrases are only tested jointly with image transformations. There are no jailbreaks, other languages or in-context recovery; ICL relearning is only cited in the Limitations.
No method is proposed or tested for robustness to recovery attacks.

missing.what: Per-model, split and method numeric results for Forget, Test, Retain and Real Celebrity sets (classification, ROUGE, factuality, cloze). These are readable for the forget and test columns and are needed to compare forgetting depth against utility loss.

Multimodal vs unimodal GA, Grad. Diff., KL and NPO differences per split. Multimodal unlearning forgets classification better; unimodal unlearning forgets generation and cloze better but collapses utility faster.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2 is flattened. The column alignment above infers test fact/cloze, then retain, then celebrity order, so verify against the PDF; Idefics2 retain classification values appear duplicated from LLaVA. Vanilla forget classification is only about 50–55%, so the fine-tuned model knew the profiles imperfectly. No uncertainty estimates are given. The system prompt is an evaluation-time prevention baseline, not a recovery attack.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that targeted accuracy reaches chance or test whether simple recovery attacks fail. It does evaluate targeted-set performance and utility.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or recovery set is applied.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of blocking access versus deleting knowledge.
Paraphrased questions are evaluated along with transformed images; the study does not isolate prompting-only recovery, or test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the listed recovery attacks.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Gradient Ascent unlearning on the Forget Set; comparison with the vanilla model

conditions.value: Forget Set; classification, generation, and cloze

rows.measure: Targeted-set performance as indicators of unlearning efficacy
rows.baseline: Vanilla model fine-tuned on the full data D for 3 epochs
rows.value: The authors report that multimodal GA has better multimodal classification unlearning, while unimodal GA performs better for generation and cloze; no numeric values are assigned here because the supplied figure/table layout does not reliably support them.
rows.note: The paper describes relative reductions in performance, but does not establish near-chance performance in these results.
rows.check: Value should carry Table 2 numbers. LLaVA 5% forget classification: vanilla 51.70%, GA 44.40%, Grad. Diff. 43.60%. Forget cloze: vanilla 25.81%, GA 17.19%. These are clear drops but far from near-chance or zero recall. The modality comparison (Fig. 3) is only bar charts.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1.1; Table 2, LLaVA-1.5-7B 5% block: Forget class. vanilla 51.70%, GA 44.40%, Grad. Diff. 43.60%; Forget cloze 25.81% vs 17.19%
source_check.problem: Fine; partial fits a 7-point drop that is far from full forgetting.

rows.subject: LLaVA
rows.operation_detail: Measures retained-set accuracy after unlearning methods
rows.measure: Trade-off between forget-set efficacy and Retain Set accuracy
rows.value: The authors report that GA has the strongest unlearning ability but causes a significant decline in Retain Set accuracy; NPO and prompting preserve Retain Set accuracy better.
rows.note: Reported as a qualitative trade-off; no individual values are assigned from the flattened figure.
rows.check: The version's 'keeps general ability' fails for GA, and the row should say so with numbers. LLaVA 5% retain classification fell 46.11%→39.09%, matching the forget drop of 51.70%→44.40%. Real-celeb classification fell 51.80%→45.56%. NPO and prompting keep utility but forget less. Read Table 2 column alignment with care given the flattened layout.

source_check.correct: state partial: the text says GA has the largest forget drop but a significant retain decline. LLaVA 5% GA: forget class. 51.70%->44.40%, retain class. 46.11%->39.09%
source_check.problem: 'absent' contradicts the stated forget drop; forgetting is present but incomplete and costly, so partial.

rows.subject: LLaVA-1.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates unlearned models on paraphrased questions and transformed images in the Test Set

conditions.value: Paraphrased or newly generated questions and transformed profile images

rows.measure: Targeted knowledge performance on transformed Test Set examples
rows.baseline: Vanilla model; numerical comparison not reliably assignable from supplied figure/table layout
rows.value: The authors describe modality-dependent unlearning results and conclude that unlearning is not consistent across multimodal and unimodal evaluations; no isolated prompting-only recovery result is reported.
rows.note: Question paraphrases are combined with image transformations, so this does not isolate prompt rephrasing as the cause of any retained knowledge.
rows.check: Should link to A, not E. Forgetting carries over to paraphrased questions combined with transformed images: LLaVA 5% GA test classification went 47.86%→38.40%, so the transformed inputs did not recover knowledge. Paraphrase and image change are confounded, and no paraphrase-only number is reported, so it cannot bear on E as a prompting-only recovery attack.

source_check.correct: state partial: LLaVA 5% Test Set class. vanilla 47.86% -> GA 38.40%, a 9.5-point drop far from full forgetting; paraphrases and image transforms are combined
source_check.locator_found: Table 2, LLaVA-1.5-7B 5% block, Test Set Class. Acc; Sections 3.4, 5.1
source_check.problem: 'observed' overstates incomplete forgetting on transformed inputs; the conclusion itself reports incomplete removal across modalities.

relationships.condition: GA and Grad. Diff. on LLaVA-1.5-7B and Idefics2-8B, 5/10/15% splits
relationships.reason: Forget accuracy stays well above zero recall (e.g., LLaVA GA 44.40% vs vanilla 51.70%). Retain and celebrity accuracy drop by a similar amount (46.11→39.09%), and reasoning and helpfulness decline (R1–R5).
relationships.display_finding: LLaVA GA target accuracy fell only from 51.70% to 44.40%, retain/celebrity accuracy fell from 46.11% to 39.09%, and reasoning and helpfulness declined.

source_check.reason: Forgetting is present but incomplete (LLaVA 5% GA 51.70->44.40%; Idefics2 53.80->36.27%) and comes with a retain and utility cost. That is incomplete and costly, not absent or reversed. All linked rows are partial.

relationships.condition: NPO, KL Minimization and system-prompting baselines
relationships.reason: These preserve retain accuracy best but forget less. For example, prompting LLaVA 5% forget classification is 46.80% vs vanilla 51.70%, and it ranks lowest on Forget and Test sets. Utility is kept only at the cost of weak forgetting (R1, R2, R4).
relationships.display_finding: NPO, KL minimization and prompting best preserved retained accuracy but forgot less; prompting left LLaVA forget classification at 46.80% versus 51.70% originally.

source_check.notes: Table 2 is flattened but can be placed (each block keeps one column order). Idefics2 5% Test and Retain class. columns repeat LLaVA 5% values (47.86/38.40; 46.11/39.09), probably a paper error. No chance level is stated, and vanilla forget accuracy is only about 49-55%. No row records the Idefics2 Test-vs-Forget gap.

statements.correction: 2410.22108 introduces MLLMU-Bench (500 fictitious + 153 celebrity profiles; LLaVA-1.5-7B, Idefics2-8B). Own LLaVA 5% results: Forget class. vanilla 51.70%, GA 44.40%, Grad. Diff. 43.60%. Test Set class. 47.86%->38.40% (GA). Retain class. 46.11%->39.09% (GA). No chance level stated. CUSE's 59.20% vanilla is not this study's figure.
statements.problem: The statement gives no numbers from this study, and every number in it is from CUSE, SafeEraser, HFRU or PPE-Bench. The one right link is that MLLMU-Bench comes from this study. Citing it (R6) as support for A misleads: its own baselines forget only in part, at a utility cost.
